n: David calls on the “mighty” — possibly heavenly beings or earthly rulers — to give glory to the Lord. Even the powerful must recognize where real power lies.

f.g: Literally “sons of God” (bene elim) — likely the heavenly hosts or angels.

n: Worship should be offered with the honor God’s name deserves, in holy attire or holy splendor.

f.g: Possibly “holy attire” or “the splendor of holiness” — worship that reflects God’s purity.

n: Now a thunderstorm rolls in from the sea. Seven times the psalm repeats “the voice of the LORD,” picturing thunder as God speaking with power over the waters.

f.g: In ancient imagery, the vast, chaotic sea — which God rules.

n: God’s voice carries both power and majesty. What he says, happens.

f.w: The voice of the LORD is powerful

n: Lebanon’s cedars were the mightiest trees known; God’s voice snaps them like twigs. Nothing proud or tall stands against him.

f.g: Tall, prized trees used in Solomon’s temple, symbols of strength and pride.

n: The storm makes whole mountains seem to leap like young animals. Sirion is another name for Mount Hermon.

f.g: The Sidonian name for Mount Hermon.
Hebrew reʾem — a wild ox, not a mythical horned horse.

n: The lightning flashes like flames split apart. God commands even the fire of the storm.

f.g: Hews out or splits flames — a picture of forked lightning.

n: The storm sweeps south into the desert, shaking the wilderness of Kadesh. God’s voice reaches from the northern mountains to the southern wilderness — the whole land.

f.g: Kadesh-barnea, in the southern wilderness where Israel camped during the Exodus.

n: The storm’s force strips forests bare and startles deer into labor. Meanwhile, in his temple, worshippers cry “Glory!”
God sits enthroned above the flood — perhaps recalling Noah’s flood. He reigns as King forever, unshaken by any storm.

f.g: Hebrew mabbul, used elsewhere only for Noah’s flood.

n: The psalm that began with thunder ends with peace. The same mighty voice that shakes the earth gives strength and peace to God’s people.
